\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 11\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Antibiotics in Cirrhotic Patients\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">All cirrhotic patients with upper GI bleeding should receive antibiotics unless  contraindicated.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to Davidson’s and Baveno portal hypertension guidelines, bacterial infection is\u003cbr>extremely common after variceal bleeding and strongly predicts:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. rebleeding,   2. Renal failure,   3. spontaneous bacterial peritonitis,   4. encephalopathy,   5. and mortality.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Common regimens include:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>1. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>2. or ciprofloxacin depending on local protocols.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 12\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The above two medications are preferred because cirrhotic patients are highly prone to\u003cbr>translocation of enteric gram-negative bacteria from the gut into the bloodstream during\u003cbr>variceal bleeding. These drugs provide strong coverage against the most common organisms\u003cbr>involved, especially Enterobacteriaceae such as E. coli and Klebsiella, which are major\u003cbr>causes of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, bacteremia, and sepsis in cirrhosis. The benefit of\u003cbr>antibiotics is not only infection prevention but also reduction in rebleeding and mortality.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanical Haemostasis Before Endoscopy\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In severe uncontrolled variceal bleeding where endoscopy is delayed or unsuccessful,\u003cbr>temporary mechanical tamponade may be required.\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 12\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 12\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Sengstaken-Blakemore Tube (SBT)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is  used for: Massive uncontrolled variceal  bleeding\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It works through balloon compression  of bleeding varices.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The tube contains:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. gastric balloon,   2. esophageal balloon,   3. and aspiration ports.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The gastric balloon is inflated first and\u003cbr>traction applied. If bleeding persists,\u003cbr>the esophageal balloon may be inflated\u003cbr>carefully.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This method provides temporary haemostasis while preparing for:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  definitive endoscopy,   •  TIPS,   •  or surgery.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">However, according to Harrison’s and ICU guidelines, balloon tamponade is only a bridge\u003cbr>therapy because it carries serious risks:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>1. aspiration,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>2. esophageal rupture,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>3. airway obstruction,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>4. mucosal necrosis.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Therefore it should be performed only by experienced clinicians with airway protection  available.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 13\u003c/div>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 13\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 13\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Endoscopic Haemostasis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Endoscopy is both: Diagnostic and Therapeutic\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to current guidelines: unstable/high-risk patients should undergo endoscopy within\u003cbr>12 hours, other patients generally within 24 hours after stabilization.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Endoscopy identifies:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. source of bleeding,\u003cbr>2. active hemorrhage,\u003cbr>3. ulcers,\u003cbr>4. varices,\u003cbr>5. visible vessels,\u003cbr>6. clots,\u003cbr>7. tumors,\u003cbr>8. and stigmata of recent bleeding.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 14\u003c/div>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>3. RISK STRATIFICATION IN UPPER GASTROINTESTINAL\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>BLEEDING\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">After initial stabilization and initiation of haemostatic therapy, the next major step in the\u003cbr>management of upper gastrointestinal bleeding is:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Risk stratification\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Risk stratification refers to systematic assessment of the patient’s likelihood of:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. ongoing bleeding,\u003cbr>2. rebleeding,\u003cbr>3. hemodynamic collapse,\u003cbr>4. need for urgent intervention,\u003cbr>5. ICU admission,\u003cbr>6. and mortality.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to international gastroenterology guidelines, risk stratification is essential because\u003cbr>upper GI bleeding ranges from mild self-limited disease to catastrophic hemorrhage with\u003cbr>multiorgan failure. Early identification of high-risk patients allows rapid escalation of care\u003cbr>and timely endoscopy. The major purposes of risk stratification are:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. determining urgency of endoscopy,\u003cbr>2. predicting mortality,\u003cbr>3. predicting rebled,\u003cbr>4. identifying patients needing ICU care,\u003cbr>5. identifying low-risk patients suitable for early discharge.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Clinical Assessment of Severity\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The first stage of risk stratification is bedside clinical evaluation. Patients at high risk often  present with:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. hypotension,\u003cbr>2. Tachycardia,\u003cbr>3. syncope,\u003cbr>4. severe anemia,\u003cbr>5. active hematemesis,\u003cbr>6. persistent melena,\u003cbr>7. altered mental status,\u003cbr>8. reduced urine output,\u003cbr>9. or ongoing transfusion requirements.\u003cbr>Clinical signs suggesting major hemorrhage include:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. systolic BP &lt;90 mmHg,   2. pulse &gt;100 bpm,   3. postural hypotension,   4. cool extremities,\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 15\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">5. Confusion,\u003cbr>6. elevated lactate,\u003cbr>7. and shock.\u003cbr>According to Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, hemodynamic instability is one\u003cbr>of the strongest predictors of severe upper GI bleeding and poor outcome.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">High-Risk Clinical Features\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Certain features indicate severe disease and need for urgent intervention. These include:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Active hematemesis\u003cbr>2. Coffee-ground vomiting with instability\u003cbr>3. Massive melena\u003cbr>4. Persistent hypotension\u003cbr>5. Ongoing blood transfusion requirement\u003cbr>6. Severe anemia\u003cbr>7. Known cirrhosis with varices\u003cbr>8. Coagulopathy\u003cbr>9. Renal failure\u003cbr>10. Elderly age\u003cbr>11. Cardiovascular disease\u003cbr>12. Hepatic encephalopathy\u003cbr>13. Shock\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients with cirrhosis are particularly high risk because they frequently develop:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>✓ recurrent bleeding,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>✓ spontaneous bacterial peritonitis,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>✓ hepatorenal syndrome,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>✓ and multiorgan failure.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">GLASGOW-BLATCHFORD SCORE (GBS)\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Glasgow-Blatchford Score is one of the most used pre-endoscopic scoring systems in upper  GI bleeding.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to gastroenterology guidelines, the GBS predicts:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">✓ need for intervention,   ✓ need for blood transfusion,\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 16\u003c/div>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 16\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 16\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">✓ need for endoscopy, and risk of\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">clinical deterioration.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The score uses:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. blood urea,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. hemoglobin,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. blood pressure,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. pulse,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">5. Melena,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">6. syncope,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">7. liver disease,\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">8. and heart failure.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Higher scores indicate:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Higher risk Patients with: GBS = 0 or 1 are\u003cbr>considered very low risk and may sometimes\u003cbr>be managed as outpatients if clinically stable.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients with higher scores usually require:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. admission,   2. urgent endoscopy,   3. and close monitoring.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The Glasgow-Blatchford Score is especially useful because it can be calculated:Before  endoscopy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Clinical Interpretation and Action Plan\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Low Risk\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">GBS = 0–1 These patients have: near-zero risk of requiring intervention, very low mortality\u003cbr>risk and low rebleeding risk.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Many may be suitable for: Outpatient management if: clinically stable, no ongoing\u003cbr>bleeding, reliable follow-up available.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Higher Risk GBS ≥2\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">These patients require: hospital admission, monitoring, early endoscopy, and possible\u003cbr>intervention. Potential interventions include:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. blood transfusion,\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 17\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. IV PPI/octreotide,   3. endoscopic Haemostasis,   4. ICU monitoring,   5. surgery or TIPS if severe.\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Very High-Risk Patients\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients with: hypotension, severe anemia, active hematemesis, ongoing transfusion\u003cbr>requirement, cirrhosis and altered mental status  are considered: High-risk UGIB and often\u003cbr>require: urgent endoscopy, HDU/ICU monitoring, and aggressive resuscitation.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">ROCKALL SCORE\u003c/h3>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 17\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,
